Congenital Tibial Deficiency
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The Jones classification describes a spectrum of deficiency, including complete absence of the
tibia, partial absence of the tibia (proximal or distal), and diastasis of the tibia/fibula.
The foot often is in equinovarus.
Preaxial polydactyly may be present.
Overview
Previously termed tibial hemimelia
Spectrum of deformity that affects the lower limb in general and the tibia in particular
Only lower-limb deficiency with a defined inheritance pattern (autosomal dominant)
Congenital tibial deficiency associated with other musculoskeletal anomalies occurs in 75% of
patients.
Epidemiology
Incidence reported as 1 per 1,000,000 live births
May be bilateral in approximately 30% patients and associated with other anomalies
Etiology
Remains largely unknown
Most cases occur spontaneously; however, autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive1
patterns have been reported.
Four distinct autosomal dominant syndromes
Tibial hemimelia–foot polydactyly–triphalangeal thumbs syndrome (Warner syndrome)
Tibial hemimelia diplopodia syndrome
Tibial hemimelia–split hand and foot syndrome

Tibial hemimelia–micromelia–trigonobrachycephaly syndrome
Natural History
60% to 79% of patients have associated congenital anomalies, with abnormalities of the hip or
hand or vertebral malformations occurring alone or in various combinations.
Associated with visceral organ involvement
Cardiac malformations, genitourinary abnormalities, gastrointestinal malformations
Classification
Jones classification: based on radiographic appearance2,3 (Figure 1)
Type I: tibia completely absent
Type Ia: femur hypoplastic
Type Ib: cartilaginous anlage present; femoral epiphysis is normal.
Type II: proximal tibial epiphysis is preserved with a short segment of the tibia; distal
epiphysis is absent.
Type III: distal epiphysis is present with a short segment of tibia; proximal epiphysis is absent.
Least common type
Type IV
Tibia is short.
Fibula is relatively longer and displaced proximally at the knee.
Diastasis of the tibia and fibula at the ankle
The Paley classification describes deficiencies and provides treatment options and a prognosis
algorithm.2
Type 1: hypoplastic nondeficient tibia with relative fibular overgrowth
Type 2: proximal and distal epiphysis present with dysplastic ankle
Type 3: tibial plafond absent or deficient
Type 4: only proximal tibia present
Type 5: complete absence of the tibia
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
3/29

Figure 1 Images show tibial deficiency. A, Illustration shows the four-part Jones classification of
tibial deficiency. B, AP radiograph of the lower extremities of a patient with the proposed type 5
tibial deficiency, which is characterized by hypoplasia of the tibia; however, the proximal and
distal tibial physes are present. (Panel A reproduced with permission from Jones D, Barnes J,
Lloyd-Roberts GC: Congenital aplasia and dysplasia of the tibia with intact fibula: Classification
and management. J Bone Joint Surg Br 1978;60[1]:31-39. Panel B reproduced with permission from
Clinton R, Birch JG: Congenital tibial deficiency: A 37-year experience at one institution. J Pediatr
Orthop 2015;35[4]:385-390.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
The typical appearance is a short tibial segment with a flexed knee and a prominent proximal
fibula. A skin dimple may be present about the proximal tibia. Commonly, the foot is in rigid
equinovarus and supination (Figure 2).
The presence or absence of active knee extension must be carefully assessed because it will
help guide management and determine prognosis. Flexion contracture of a variable degree is
almost always present.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
4/29

A proximal tibia anlage may be present but not apparent on early radiographs because of
delayed ossification.
Associated musculoskeletal anomalies (cleft hand associated with tibial deficiency) occur and
must be evaluated.
Recommend genetics consultation and advance imaging studies to evaluate for other organ
dysfunction.
Figure 2 Photograph of the lower extremities of an infant shows the typical clinical appearance of
tibial deficiency. (Reproduced from Krajbich JI: Lower-limb deficiencies and amputations in
children. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[6]:358-367.)
Patient History
Commonly, patients are initially referred to orthopaedics for equinovarus foot positioning,
which may be confused with isolated clubfoot.
Physical Examination
Fully evaluate both lower extremities, the hips, and the spine.
Findings vary depending on the presence or absence of the tibia.
Jones type 1a
Hamstring function generally is present but quadriceps is deficient.
Knee flexion contracture
Knee positioned proximal and lateral to the femoral condyle
Patella often is absent.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
5/29

Foot has rigid equinovarus.
Jones type 1b and type 2
Hamstring and quadriceps are normal.
Fibular head displaced proximally and laterally
Limb is in varus position with varus instability.
Equinovarus foot
Jones type 3
Knee is unstable, with extra digits distally.
Varus deformity of the leg
Jones type 4
Knee stable
Diastasis of the distal tibia and fibula
Foot is in rigid equinovarus.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
A proximal tibia anlage may be present but not apparent on early radiographs because of
delayed ossification. An early clue to the absence of the proximal tibia is a small and minimally
ossified distal femoral epiphysis.
Ultrasonography
May be used to identify a cartilaginous tibial anlage
Can identify if a patellar tendon and a functioning quadriceps mechanism are present
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
May be useful in determining if knee reconstruction is feasible and for preoperative planning
Management
Based on the presence of a stable knee with a functional extensor mechanism4 (Table 1)
Goal in reconstruction is to attain a functional limb equal in length to the normal limb at
maturity and a stable, plantigrade and flexible foot.

Multiple staged procedures must be anticipated, especially in patients who undergo limb
salvage.

deficiencies, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1423-1436.
Surgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Knee disarticulation and prosthesis
Reconstruction
Tibiofibular synostosis is effective at extending a short proximal tibia segment.
The Brown procedure (centralization of the fibula under the femur to manage complete tibial
absence) is associated with a high failure rate and is not recommended.
Newer reconstructive options have been described for reconstruction, especially for Paley
type 2, type 3, and type 4.
Preoperative Planning
All patients should be screened for associated anomalies before surgical treatment is initiated.
Surgical Approaches
Type Ia
Knee disarticulation and prosthetic management preferred over above-knee amputation
Type 1b and type 2
Tibiofibular synostosis

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
7/29

If a functional ankle cannot be attained, a Syme or similar partial amputation can be
performed.
Type 3
Syme or Chopart amputation
Type 4
Modified Syme disarticulation when the child reaches walking age
Lengthening and reconstruction may be possible if a stable plantigrade foot can be attained.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Timing of surgical management
Engaging the family at the initial consultation in a discussion on treatment options
Complications
Pain
16% of patients report moderate pain with prostheses.5
Outcomes
Health-related quality of life in children aged 8 to 18 years does not differ from the reference
value.
Fibular Deficiency
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Previously termed and also known as fibular hemimelia
Represents a spectrum of pathology ranging from minimal limb-length inequality to severe
shortening of the affected side, with foot, ankle, and tibia deformities
Femur also may be affected.
Epidemiology
Most common long bone deficiency
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
8/29

Incidence of 1 to 2 per 100,000 live births
Bilateral in 9% to 52% of patients1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Tibia may be shortened and bowed with apex anteromedial.
Fibular absence is variable.
Other associated abnormalities include femoral shortening/deficiency, progressive/recurrent
genu valgum, cruciate deficiencies of the knee, tarsal coalitions, ball-and-socket ankle joint,
deficient lateral rays, and ulnar deficiencies in the upper extremity.
Etiology
Etiology is unclear.
Sporadic appearance is the most common; however, chromosomal abnormalities with
autosomal dominant, recessive, and X-linked transmissions have been reported.
Part of a spectrum of anomalies believed to be related to a defect in the femoral-fibular-ulnar
developmental field.
Classification
Three classification systems currently are used.
Achterman and Kalamchi classification system: describes the spectrum of deficiency ranging
from shortened fibula to complete absence of the fibula1
Type 1: fibula present but hypoplastic
Type 1a: proximal fibula physis distal to the proximal tibia physis; and distal fibula physis
proximal to talar dome.
Type 1b: 30% to 50% less length proximally and no distal support for the ankle joint
Type 2: complete absence of fibula
Birch classification system: matches clinical findings with treatment recommendations.
Type 1: foot reconstructible (≥3 rays)
Type 1a: limb-length discrepancy (LLD) of less than 6%
Type 1b: LLD of 6% to 10%
Type 1c: LLD of 11% to 30%
Type 1d: LLD of greater than 30%
Type 2: foot not reconstructible
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
9/29

Paley classification: treatment decisions based on the clinical and radiographic appearance
of the foot and ankle rather than LLD (Figure 3)
Type 1: tibial shortening with normal ankle
Type 2: tibial shortening with dynamic valgus ankle
Type 3: fixed equinovalgus ankle
Type 3a: equinovalgus of distal tibia, normal subtalar joint
Type 3b: normal distal tibia, subtalar coalition in equinovalgus
Type 3c: distal tibia and subtalar joint with fixed deformities
Type 4: fixed equinovarus (clubfoot type)
Figure 3 Illustration shows the Paley classification of fibular hemimelia. Type 1 consists of a
stable ankle. Type 2 consists of dynamic ankle valgus. Type 3 involves a fixed equinovalgus ankle
deformity, with 3a being ankle type, 3b being subtalar type, and 3c being combined
ankle/subtalar type. Type 4 involves a fixed equinovarus ankle (clubfoot type) (Reproduced with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
10/29

permission from Paley D: Surgical reconstruction for fibular hemimelia. J Child Orthop
2016;10[6]:557-583.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
The classic appearance is a short limb with an equinovalgus foot and skin dimpling over the
midanterior tibia (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustration of a 13-year-old child shows the anomalies associated with congenital fibular
deficiency. (Reproduced from Hamdy RC, Makhdom AM, Saran N, Birch J: Congenital fibular
deficiency. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[4]:246-255.)
Patient History
Ask about a family history of limb deficiency.
Ask about potential toxic exposures and other possible prenatal events.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
11/29

Evaluate the upper extremity for any limb deficiency or abnormality (Figure 5).
Then, fully evaluate the entire lower extremities, the hips, and the spine.
Hip: evaluate for contractures and/or asymmetric range of motion (ROM); a hip with femoral
deficiency typically is flexed, abducted, and externally rotated.
Knee—Evaluate for valgus deformity, full ROM, patellar stability, and cruciate stability.
Leg: evaluate for shortening and bowing compared with other side; may observe a dimple on
the anterior tibia at apex of the deformity.
Ankle—Evaluate ROM/stability compared with that of the contralateral side.
Foot: count number of rays and evaluate subtalar motion and suppleness of foot; determine
if the foot can be positioned plantigrade or whether a fixed or dynamic equinovalgus (or
equinovarus) deformity is present.
Figure 5 Images show fibular deficiency. Photographs of the left lower extremity (A) and both
lower extremities (B)of a patient show a shortened limb, an equinovalgus foot, and dimpling over
the anterior tibia. C, Lateral radiograph of the left lower extremity shows absence of the fibula
and bowing of the tibia. (Reproduced from Scaduto AA, Frost NL: Pediatric lower extremity
deformities and limb deficiencies, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review,
ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1423-1436.)
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The fibula is short or absent, and anteromedial bowing of the tibia may be present.
Fibula physes are displaced from their natural levels; proximally they are distal to the tibial
physis, and distally they are proximal to the talar dome.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
12/29

The intercondylar notch of the femur typically is shallow, and the tibial spines are small or
absent (indicating an absent anterior cruciate ligament).
Foot radiographs may not initially demonstrate a tarsal coalition. They will demonstrate absent
lateral rays (if applicable).
Over time, the ankle may develop a spherical shape from accommodation of the tarsal
coalition.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may aid in planning ankle reconstruction to determine if a tarsal coalition is present and
the extent of the coalition.
MRI also can determine cruciate deficiency if the physical examination is equivocal.
MRI typically is used as a planning tool for patients undergoing soft-tissue reconstruction of
the knee or ankle.
Ultrasonography
Prenatal ultrasonography can detect most upper and lower limb deficiencies; however, they
may be undiagnosed in 20% to 25% of prenatal patients.
Management
Management is guided by the severity of the discrepancy and the functionality of the foot. This
is guided by the Birch or the Paley classification system.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications/Contraindications
If total LLD projects to less than 2 cm at skeletal maturity and no fixed foot/ankle deformity is
present, then surgical management may not be indicated. This would be rare.
Contraindications to nonsurgical management are a projected LLD greater than 2 cm at
maturity and/or a fixed foot/ankle deformity.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperatively, and in between surgical procedures, management with lifts, orthotics, and
various prostheses is common.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
13/29

Treatment options include but are not limited to internal shoe lifts, external shoe lifts,
supramalleolar orthoses to control the subtalar joint, ankle-foot orthoses to control equinus,
and a foot-on-foot prosthesis for larger limb-length differences.
Surgical Management
Indications
Indications for the management of fibular deficiency include greater than 2 cm LLD at skeletal
maturity with or without a fixed foot/ankle deformity.
The goal of surgical management, regardless whether limb ablation or limb reconstruction, is
to attain minimal limb-length difference, maximal function, and minimal pain.
Reconstruction principles for management of fibular hemimelia center on achieving a
functional limb; near normal limb length; and a plantigrade, stable, and flexible foot at
maturity.
Treatment also is specific to the patient, with ablation and/or reconstruction attempts
performed at centers that have extensive experience with such treatment.
Contraindications
Surgical treatment is contraindicated in patients who are not healthy enough for surgical
treatment and general anesthesia.
In addition, if limb ablation has been recommended but the patient’s family is not ready for
such treatment or it is against religious or cultural beliefs, then surgical treatment may be
contraindicated.
Ablation also may be contraindicated in patients with nonfunctional upper extremities.
Techniques/Procedures
The most common surgical procedures performed to manage fibular deficiency include the
following:
Limb ablation
Syme amputation
Boyd amputation
Limb reconstruction
SUPERankle reconstruction
SHORDT procedure
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
14/29

Limb-lengthening surgery
Epiphysiodesis
Hemiepiphysiodesis
Preoperative Planning
First, evaluate the function of the hip, knee, and ankle, along with the projected LLD.
For ablation, the ideal age is the time at which the patient is standing and attempting to walk.
For patients who can stand independently, obtaining long-length radiographs with a block
under the short limb to level the pelvis is very useful. This can help determine current LLD and
also evaluate for mechanical axis deviation, which is quite common.
For patients on a reconstruction track, multiple surgical procedures often are necessary.
Typically, soft-tissue reconstruction procedures, or preparatory surgical procedures, are
performed to place the joint in a more functional position followed by limb lengthening
thereafter. A life plan should be created before reconstruction to determine the optimal timing
of surgical procedures during the patient’s childhood.
Treatment Based on Classification Systems
Birch type 1a and 1b—For a plantigrade foot with minimal LLD, shoe lift alone may be a
sufficient treatment option. A well-timed contralateral epiphysiodesis may be helpful for
patients who do not desire to undergo lifelong shoe lift treatment.
Birch type 1c and 1d—The decision to pursue limb reconstruction rather than ablation should
consider the beliefs of the family and patient, the functionality of the foot, and the number of
surgical procedures necessary to achieve near-equal limb lengths.
Limb ablation—Syme and Boyd amputation have been used with good success.
If the stump too long: distal tibia/fibula epiphysiodesis
If the stump too short: lengthening of the stump
May require hemiepiphysiodesis to correct angular deformities during growth
Limb reconstruction
The first treatment goal is to create a plantigrade foot. The Paley classification system may
be useful to evaluate the location of the foot and ankle deformity and also may guide
management. Management usually involves SUPERankle reconstruction or a SHORDT
procedure. SUPER is an acronym for Systematic Utilitarian Procedure for Extremity
Reconstruction. This procedure achieves a stable plantigrade (90°) foot and ankle that can
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
15/29

be placed flat on the ground. A SHORDT (SHortening Osteotomy Realignment Distal Tibia)
procedure corrects dynamic valgus of the ankle.
Limb lengthening is performed via distraction osteogenesis. Multiple techniques are
available for limb lengthening, including lengthening via an external fixator or an internal
lengthening device.
Lengthening should be limited to 15% to 20% of the length of the bone because
complication rates rise substantially after this level.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Limb lengthening and reconstruction should be performed at major centers that have
experience with such procedures. Complications include but are not limited to joint
dislocations, joint stiffness, bone infection, and malalignment after lengthening.
Limb ablation should be discussed thoroughly with the family before proceeding with the
procedure. Ensure that the patient’s upper extremities have adequate function before
ablation. Also ensure that skilled prosthetists and physical therapists are available in the
region to assist the patient and family after limb ablation.
Complications
Limb ablation—Limb ablation may be associated with stump irritation. Angular deformities
and/or contractures may necessitate additional surgical procedures, and additional
procedures to optimize stump length also may be necessary.
Limb reconstruction—Complications include joint subluxation/dislocation, joint contracture,
nerve injury, nonunion/malunion, or osteomyelitis.
Outcomes
Adults who have undergone amputation for fibular deficiency as children have an average to
above-average quality of life compared with that of the able adult population.
These adults report increased prevalence of chronic pain and early retirement.
Proximal Femur Focal Deficiency
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064

Overview
Proximal femur focal deficiency (PFFD) and congenital short femur represent a spectrum of
femoral hypoplasia (Table 2).
Congenital femur deficiency (CFD) represents a more comprehensive description of femoral
deficiency.
PFFD is a specific subset within CFD in which the deficiency mainly is proximal.

American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1423-1436.
Epidemiology
Incidence of 0.5 to 2 per 100,000 live births
Considered a failure of formation and is grouped under transverse deficiencies
Bilateral in 15% of patients
Ipsilateral foot and lower-limb anomalies are present in as many as 70% of patients.
Etiology
Exact etiology unknown
Sclerotome subtraction theory
Early damage to neural crest cells that ultimately form the L4 and L5 sensory roots may play
a role in the development of CFD.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
17/29

Chondrocyte proliferation defect theory
Defects in chondrocyte proliferation in proximal femoral physis may be caused by
ischemia/hypoxia, irradiation, toxins, hormones, or mechanical/thermal injury.
Natural History
Associated ipsilateral limb anomalies include knee laxity with deficiency of the cruciate
ligaments, fibular hemimelia, and absent lateral rays.
Classification
The Aitken classification system is based on radiographic appearance6 (Figure 6).
Class A:
Proximal femur: at or above the level of the acetabulum
Head ossification: delayed but occurs; coxa vara
Neck ossification: delayed but occurs
Well-formed acetabulum
Class B:
Proximal femur: above the level of the acetabulum
Head ossification: delayed but occurs; coxa vara
Neck ossification: does not occur
Acetabulum dysplastic
Class C:
Femoral head absent
Severe acetabular dysplasia
Class D:
No proximal femur is observed.
Small tuft of bone observed proximal to distal femoral physis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
18/29

Figure 6 Diagram shows the Aitken classification of proximal focal femoral deficiency. (Adapted
with permission from Herring JA: Pediatric Orthopaedics, ed 4. Philadelphia, PA, WB Saunders,
2007.)
The Paley classification system categorizes CFD according to treatment recommendations.
Type 1: intact femur with a mobile hip and knee
Type 1a: normal ossification of the femoral head and neck
Type 1b: delayed ossification, subtrochanteric type
Type 1c: delayed ossification, neck type
Type 2: mobile pseudarthrosis with a mobile knee
Type 2a: femoral head mobile in the acetabulum
Type 2b: femoral head absent or stiff in the acetabulum

19/29

Type 3: diaphyseal deficiency of the femur
Knee motion greater or equal to 45°
Knee motion less than 45°
Complete absence of the femur
Type 4: distal deficiency of femur

Classification
Multiple classification schemes exist for CFD and PFFD. The two most commonly used
classification systems are the Aitken and Paley classifications. The Aitken classification
system is specific for PFFD, whereas the Paley classification system is specific for CFD.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
In patients with CFD, the femur is short and typically presents as flexed, abducted, and
externally rotated (Figure 7).
The entire lower extremity should be evaluated for associated anomalies.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
20/29

Figure 7 Clinical photograph of a child with a proximal femur focal deficiency. The ankle of the
affected extremity is almost at the level of the contralateral knee. The foot on the affected side is
almost normal. This child would be a good candidate for knee fusion and rotationplasty.
(Reproduced from Krajbich JI: Lower-limb deficiencies and amputations in children. J Am Aced
Orthop Surg 1998;6[6]:358-367.)
Patient History
Ask about family history of limb deficiency.
Ask about potential toxic exposures and other possible prenatal events.
Physical Examination
First, evaluate the upper extremity for any limb deficiency or abnormality.
Then, fully evaluate the entire lower extremities, hips, and spine.
Hip: evaluate for contractures and/or asymmetric ROM; a hip with femoral deficiency
typically is flexed, abducted, and externally rotated.
Knee—Evaluate for valgus deformity, full ROM, patellar stability, and cruciate stability.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:37 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Lower Extremity Deformities and Limb Deficiencies
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004064
21/29

Leg—Evaluate for associated fibular deficiency and for shortening and bowing compared
with the contralateral side.
Ankle—Evaluate ROM/stability and ensure adequate dorsiflexion.
Foot—Count number of rays and evaluate subtalar motion and suppleness of the foot.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Before standing age, an AP and lateral radiograph of both femurs and tibias with the legs
pulled straight and patella pulled forward may be helpful. A separate AP pelvis radiograph also
may be beneficial.
Typical radiographic appearance may include the following:
Femur is short.
Femoral head may/may not be present.
Lucency in neck or subtrochanteric area, which may represent delayed ossification
Varying degrees of acetabular dysplasia
Coxa vara proximally
Distal femoral condyles may be hypoplastic.
Associated fibular deficiency
Computed Tomography
May be helpful in older adolescents with continued/recurrent acetabular dysplasia to better
elucidate the morphology
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
May be useful for the following:
Determining proximal femur anatomy at a young age

The management of CFD is multifactorial. Each child should be treated individual and may
benefit from a multidisciplinary team that focuses on treatment options, including shoe lifts,
orthotics, prostheses, physical therapy, and surgical management. All these treatment options
are designed to maximize function.
First, the surgeon must determine if the limb is reconstructible. Factors that should be
considered before performing reconstruction include the stability and morphology of the hip,
knee, and ankle joints and the projected limb-length difference. Candidates for reconstruction
candidate should have stable joints or joints that can be reconstructed and an acceptable
amount of limb-length difference to make up at skeletal maturity.
Nonsurgical Management
Children with CFD will require nonsurgical treatment as a part of their lifetime treatment plan.
Observation, education, orthotic and prosthetic fitting, and physical therapy are performed
before surgical management or in between surgical procedures.
Surgical Management
Indications
The Paley classification system addresses surgical treatment recommendations for each type
of femoral deficiency (Figure 8). 
Type 1: intact femur with mobile hip and knee
Can be addressed via limb reconstruction
Joint preparation surgery must be addressed before lengthening. Procedures may include
hip and/or knee stabilization surgical procedures known as SUPERhip and SUPERknee
reconstructions.
Limb lengthenings are then spread out as long as possible to decrease stress to the child
and the family—a minimum of 4 years between lengthening procedures if possible.
Contralateral epiphysiodesis may be helpful to decrease the amount of lengthening
necessary.
The patient may require hemiepiphysiodesis to address genu valgum on more than one
occasion during childhood.
Type 2: mobile pseudarthrosis with a mobile knee
Type 2a: Femoral head mobile in the acetabulum; these patients can be treated in a fashion
relatively similar to patients with a type 1 femur. The femoral head and neck must be

ossified before pursuing limb lengthening.
Type 2b: Femoral head absent or stiff in acetabulum; may consider lengthening along with
a pelvic support osteotomy.
Type 3: diaphyseal deficiency of the femur
Syme amputation or Van Ness rotationplasty may be considered for severely shortened
femurs.
Type 4: distal deficiency of the femur
This is the rarest type of deficiency.
If reconstruction of the knee joint is possible to a more stable position, then knee
reconstruction followed by lengthening may be possible.
Limb modification surgery
If deficiency of the femur is too severe, the joint is too deficient to allow for successful
lengthening, or the patient’s family does not wish to pursue lengthening, then some type of
limb modification typically is indicated.
May include arthrodesis of hip or knee or pelvis support osteotomy
The main goal of limb modification is to have the ankle at the level of the contralateral knee
at skeletal maturity.
Limb ablation consists of foot ablation with Syme or Boyd techniques.
Optimal age for amputation is 10 months to 2 years.
Early amputation is avoided if severe upper extremity deficiencies require the use of the
feet for activities of daily living.
Syme versus Boyd amputation
The Syme amputation (ankle disarticulation) is simple procedure and accommodates a
tapered prosthesis at the ankle for optimal cosmesis.
The Boyd amputation, in which the calcaneus is retained and fused to the distal tibia,
prevents heel pad migration, aids prosthesis suspension, and may provide better end-
bearing. It also may limit prosthetic foot options because of its greater length.

1: intact femur with a mobile hip and knee. Type 2: proximal femur pseudarthrosis with a mobile
hip and knee. Type 3: diaphyseal deficiency of the femur with an absent hip joint and a mobile

Rotationplasty (Figure 9)
The lower extremity is rotated 180° through the remaining femur and/or fused tibia to allow
the ankle joint to function as a knee. The foot functions as a residual tibia similar to a below-
knee amputation.
The patient must have a mobile and sensate foot.
Poor results may be associated with fibular deficiency and three or fewer foot rays.

Complications
Limb modification and ablation—Limb ablation may be associated with stump irritation.
Angular deformities and/or contractures may necessitate additional surgical procedures, and
additional procedures to optimize stump length also may be necessary. Van Ness
rotationplasty is associated with a unique set of complications, including neurovascular
injuries and recurrence/reversal of rotation over time.
Limb reconstruction—Complications may include joint subluxation/dislocation, joint
contracture, nerve injury, nonunion/malunion, or osteomyelitis.
Outcomes
Outcome studies support limb modification and limb reconstruction approaches in patients
with femoral deficiency.
Outcomes may be institution dependent because limb modification and reconstruction
techniques are complex and best served via a multidisciplinary team.
